For the Chialoup de Toorpruis, Batavia, Governor General and the most noble gentlemen of the Council of the Dutch Indies; — Most noble, strict, greatly esteemed, mighty, wise, prudent, and most generous sir and gentlemen. The Chialoup de Troonprins on the 30th of March last arrived safely here at the roadstead with the second [officer] destined for this government, and with it we received the first fateful news of the ship Tiessenburg, the circumstances of which have been described at length in a statement from various sailors, along with two letters from the governor Breton, which conveyed the contents, papers, linens, and slaves, and some other minor items which we received via the aforementioned vessel assisted by the panjallang [type of vessel] de Snuffelaar, completely, and the last-mentioned small vessel has already departed for Ternate. We live in the hope that the ministers of Makassar will have already arranged the necessary means for what remained on Buton under the supervision of the ship's captain and steersman, as well as for the retrieval of the ship's crew. And since the bearer of this has received orders from your most noble excellencies to return to Batavia upon first arrival, we have deemed it fitting to report to you in all respect that the Voorland sailed in on the 16th of January at night with a fresh breeze, and the Standvastigheid on the 21st of February was towed in by the force of Orembaaij, having received with it besides the further cargo 39 2k [uncertain: measurement or quantity] of provisions, and this necessity compelled us already on the 13th of March to determine the distribution of rice for everyone without distinction at 20 pounds [modern equivalent: approximately 9 kilograms] for each person per month. Under these circumstances we humbly beseech that your most noble excellencies will be pleased to grant us early relief of 1000 lasts [modern equivalent: approximately 1,000 tons], since our entire supply amounts to no more than approximately 400 lasts, and among the private individuals there is very little

Now with the flowing stones appearing without any noise or visible violence, the hill in front of the land of the widow Courwal rose very strongly, a great multitude of stones fell here about into the water, and the reef at low water was as if flooded with them. Moreover, the water here and there was continuously washed ashore with a vapor rushing over it like a pot of boiling water over fire, and the water itself extended to a distance of more than 20 rods [modern equivalent: approximately 100 meters] from the wall, so that one could not hold one's hand in it for three counts, although the extension of that hill northward since that time not only made no progress but also the glow which was previously so strong on this hill diminished greatly. Following this rain, the eruption at the foot of the aforementioned hill was accompanied with greater force, and indeed in such a manner that in a few days the passage opposite the wharf became narrowed by more than 50 rods [modern equivalent: approximately 250 meters], and truly this sorrowful sight must strike every heart and cause one to firmly establish that if this fire were to continue to break through in three ways for merely two more weeks, then the passage between the mountain and the wharf would be stopped up with stones and Neira through the advancing fire would be transformed into a heap of ruins. Since the 17th of September, the fury of the volcano and the rolling off of stones and the fire itself became extraordinarily quiet, with only a small smoke remaining visible above the slope, and the daily ejections from the first opening diminished, and at the end of this month ceased entirely, to the great relief of the Neira inhabitants. Then, as the fire gained more space through the new opening, it caused a prolonged fire both on the south and on the north side beneath the trees that had remained undamaged until then. However, at the same time the steady fire in the middle of the mountain was completely extinguished. With the breaking of the west monsoon, one fell into a well-founded fear of the suffering from ash and contagious sicknesses. The first was indeed so abundant now and then that precautions were taken everywhere regarding the wells and water supplies. However, not with the further consequences that the old histories contain in similar circumstances. In the meantime, already two-thirds of the fire mountain on the Neira side have been transformed into ravines, small hills, and piled-up burned-out stones. The trees have been burned with branch, trunk, and root, and consequently also the feared distress from the west monsoon continues. Furthermore, the subsidence of the mountain is so great that one must now step back 17 floor-stones further from the observation point of the same on the inner courtyard of Castle Nassau [Casteel Nassauw] in comparison to before. The undersigned, taking the liberty at this opportunity with all due respect to lay before Your High Excellencies his grievances concerning criminal sentences without distinction, for according to the dictate of the paternal order of the year 1759 and a resolution taken thereupon in the Council of India on the 25th of February 1741, no sentences involving corporal punishment, according to the ancient orders in India, may be carried out for execution before they have been approved by the Governor or the chief authority. Yet against this, a bandage-like custom has been imposed to extend this otherwise necessary approval to all criminal sentences without distinction, indeed even to civil decrees and executions. Through this extension, a commander very often comes to fall under the unpleasant suspicions of partiality, harshness, and persecution on the one hand, while on the other side, through the consequence of the approval of all responsibility for committed irregularities and oversights, he believes himself to be completely free. The undersigned is willing to concede this under the determination of the aforementioned extracts, considering that it is then his duty to examine the case carefully and to consider whether and to what extent the sentence named above would conform to the best knowledge. However, in a lesser degree of justice, and when matters can be settled through an ordinary process, he believes, under correction of wiser opinion, that such political approval is improper, as it causes a subordinate judge to deviate from the otherwise customary precautions if the responsibility remains upon him.
